podcast.body: Bono missed his wife Ali's birthday while immersed in sessions for The Joshua Tree (1986) and attempted to make amends by writing a love song. The band was unimpressed; Bono admits he is not good at simple love songs. The song was relegated to the B-side of the 12-inch of "Where the Streets Have No Name" (one of The Joshua Tree's major singles), where it lay mostly forgotten for over a decade. For the 1998 greatest hits collection, the band revisited it, rewrote it, added chords, changed the vocals, re-recorded it, and released it as a single with a video shot in St. Stephen's Green, Dublin, featuring members of Boyzone at Ali's request plus the Chip and Dale Dancers. All royalties from the song go to the Chernobyl Children's Project, a group that funds trips for children out of the contaminated zone. "Bono threw in the Chip and Dale dancers as a bit of a bonus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was originally written by Bono for his wife after he forgot her birthday. The 1987 original version appeared as a bonus track on the 12-inch and later CD single for "Where The Streets Have No Name" but did not make it onto "The Joshua Tree" album. It was eventually re-recorded and released as a standalone single. "Bono wrote for his wife when he forgot her birthday. It was eventually we recorded and released as a single on its own, but here is the 1987 original. I'm losing you, yeah. I love the sweetest thing you've ever heard. The sweetest thing."

podcast.body: This song, originally left off The Joshua Tree, was written by Bono for his wife, Allie, after he forgot her birthday during the album's recording. Allie claimed the publishing rights as a gift and donated them to a Ukrainian Chernobyl charity. Initially a B-side for "Where the Streets Have No Name" in 1987, it gained significant radio airplay. Re-recorded and re-released in 1998, it became a number one hit in Canada and Ireland, reached number six in the UK, but only number 63 in the US. In Europe, the 1998 single was promoted with gold-foiled "sweetest thing chocolate bars," now coveted collector's items. "The original recording of the Sweetest Thing rejected for inclusion on the Joshua Tree, but a big hit as a stand-alone single when it was re-recorded more than a decade later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
